extracted.intended_audience: aspiring freelance magazine writers and journalists pitching feature stories
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and concrete criteria for pitching and landing magazine feature assignments, focused on first-time/early-career freelancers aiming to break into magazine 'well' sections. Covers what to include in a pitch, packaging, timing, and relationship-building with editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with the FOB / pitch shorter pieces first
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors advise new writers to begin with front-of-book (FOB) assignments and shorter pieces before attempting features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major publications often assign features to proven freelancers who have written FOB pieces and understand the brand. Building a track record in FOB departments helps editors trust you with larger feature work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include News and Numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Give an old topic fresh life by incorporating a timely angle such as a new study, statistic, or recent development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compelling data can create urgency and push editors to publish sooner. Use sources such as EurekAlert (scientific studies), PR Newswire (corporate announcements), Google Trends (popular search topics), and regional publications for stories with national appeal. Pro Tip: The story doesn't need to be the latest development, but a timely angle can secure the assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add an Anecdote
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a personal story or anecdote in your pitch to help readers connect emotionally and to show that you've done outreach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes demonstrate commitment and that you've invested time in the concept. A strong anecdote proves you can connect with the audience, find compelling sources, and tell stories that resonate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Package Your Pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that you've thought about the complete package beyond the prose—how the story could appear in the magazine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include brief suggestions for visual or structural elements (fact boxes with key statistics, resource lists, sidebar suggestions, photo or video opportunities). Keep packaging recommendations concise (just a few sentences); editors don't want the whole story before they're intrigued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nail the Headline
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a compelling headline that matches the publication's style and helps sell the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective headlines create urgency (e.g., 'The Dangers of Missing Breakfast'), challenge assumptions ('Is Sleeping Making You Fat?'), or use numbers ('5 Ways to...'). Even if the headline is changed in print, including one shows professionalism and thoroughness; a standout headline alone can sometimes secure an assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go Beyond an Idea — show tone and approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Write your pitch in the story’s actual tone or include the opening paragraphs so editors can envision the piece and evaluate your writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing the first few paragraphs as if they were the article can help land bylines, though it takes more upfront work. If you don't want to write that much, instead demonstrate your research: list confirmed interview sources, show research depth, and mention any exclusive access opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sell Yourself — explain why you're the right writer
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain your unique qualifications for the assignment so editors understand why you should be hired to write the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualifications can include personal experience with the topic, industry connections, specialized knowledge, geographic advantage, or social media following. Treat the pitch as a business pitch—describe how you'll help promote the finished piece, your ability to drive traffic, and your social reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show confirmed sources and research depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that you've done preliminary reporting by listing confirmed interviewees and evidence of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioning confirmed sources and research depth reassures editors that the story is feasible and that you’ve invested time. This can substitute for writing opening paragraphs if you prefer not to draft prose in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the pitch concise (length & content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitches should generally be brief—typically 3–4 paragraphs that include the hook, why it's timely, your approach, and why you're qualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness helps busy editors quickly evaluate the idea. Include the essential elements (hook, timeliness, approach, qualifications) without long exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not simultaneously pitch the exact same story
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid simultaneous identical submissions to multiple publications; wait until one publication has passed before querying another with the same idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may pitch different angles of the same topic to different publications, and if one publication passes you can tweak and pitch elsewhere as long as the story remains unpublished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: If you don’t hear back, follow up once after 1–2 weeks, then move on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No response typically means no interest. A single follow-up is appropriate; persistence over time (regular pitching to target magazines) builds name recognition but repeated immediate follow-ups are not advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target the right editor / find appropriate contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the correct section editor or contact to receive your pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the magazine’s masthead for section editors, review the website’s contributor guidelines, or use databases like MediaBistro Jobs to find current contact information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think visually and offer media opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggest photo or video opportunities and other visual elements that enhance the story’s magazine suitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual opportunities can make a pitch more attractive to editors; include them succinctly as part of the pitch packaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand editorial calendars, timing, and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that timing, editorial calendars, and budgets affect whether a pitch gets accepted, independent of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing must be right for the magazine; even excellent pitches can be rejected for scheduling or budget reasons. Regular pitching and persistence can help you land assignments over time.
